title: Root-subgroup power laws and dual lattice maps for general isogenies
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Write $\mathbf G_a$ and $\mathbf G_m$ for [def-sc-gm-ga]. Faithfully flat means that extension of scalars along the coordinate-algebra map is exact and detects zero modules. Let $A,D$ be reductive, meaning smooth and connected with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup; unipotent means unipotent matrices in a faithful representation at geometric points. Let $T_A\subseteq A$ and $T_D\subseteq D$ be split maximal tori, and use their character lattices, cocharacter lattices, roots and coroots as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Use the root subgroups $U_\alpha$ and their isomorphisms $u_\alpha:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U_\alpha$ as in [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. Let $f:A\to D$ be faithfully flat with finite scheme-theoretic kernel, where finite means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra, and suppose $f(T_A)\subseteq T_D$. Set $f_T=f|_{T_A}$, $f^*(\chi)=\chi\circ f_T$, and $f_*(\nu)=f_T\circ\nu$. The map $f_T:T_A\to T_D$ is faithfully flat with finite kernel, and $f^*$ is injective with finite cokernel. There is a bijection $\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta$ from the roots of $A$ to the roots of $D$, numbers $e_\alpha$ that are powers of the characteristic exponent of $F$ (the exponent is $1$ in characteristic zero), and $c_\alpha\in F^\times$, such that $$f^*\beta=e_\alpha\alpha,\qquad f_*(\alpha^\vee)=e_\alpha\beta^\vee,\qquad f(u_\alpha(a))=u_\beta(c_\alpha a^{e_\alpha}).$$ The last identity holds for every commutative $F$-algebra and every element $a$ of that algebra, for any chosen root parametrizations with suitable $c_\alpha$. In particular $f(U_\alpha)=U_\beta$ as subgroup schemes. The kernel of $f$ is central if and only if every $e_\alpha=1$; central means commuting with all group elements after every scalar extension.

source.place: Definitions 23.1--23.2, printed pp.483--484, and Proposition 23.5 with its proof, printed pp.485--486, especially formula (146) over every test algebra and the final centrality criterion. No Borel compatibility is asserted here.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-quotient-borel-torus-images], the scheme-theoretic image of $T_A$ is a maximal torus of $D$ and the map to it is faithfully flat. It is contained in $T_D$, hence equals $T_D$. The kernel of $f_T$ is the closed subgroup $T_A\cap\ker f$ of the finite scheme $\ker f$, hence finite. Write $X_A=X^*(T_A)$ and $X_D=X^*(T_D)$. By [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality] and [lem-sfb-split-torus-hom-matrices], these are finite free lattices and $f_T$ is the map of split diagonalizable groups induced by $h=f^*:X_D\to X_A$. Faithful flatness makes the coordinate map $F[X_D]\to F[X_A]$ injective, so $h$ is injective: a nonzero element of its kernel would identify two distinct group-algebra basis vectors. The coordinate ring of $\ker f_T$ is $F[X_A]/(e_{h(x)}-1:x\in X_D)=F[\operatorname{coker}h]$. Its finite dimension says that $\operatorname{coker}h$ is finite. In particular $h_{\mathbf Q}$ is an isomorphism and the two torus ranks agree.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, first two sentences of proof, p.485; Theorem 12.9, pp.233--234.

proof.text: Fix a root $\alpha$ of $A$ and a parametrization $u_\alpha$. Factor $f\circ u_\alpha:\mathbf G_a\to D$ through its closed image $I$ using [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization]. Its kernel $N_\alpha$ is a finite closed subgroup of $\mathbf G_a$, so it is proper. The quotient identification in [lem-sfb-additive-subgroup-polynomial-quotient] identifies $I$ with $\mathbf G_a$ and the quotient map with a monic additive polynomial $P$ of positive degree $n$. Conjugation by $T_A$ preserves $N_\alpha$, by normality of $\ker f$ and the root conjugation formula in [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. The equivariant clause of the polynomial-quotient node says that, in this coordinate on $I$, conjugation through $f_T(t)$ is multiplication by $\alpha(t)^n$, on every test algebra. Since $f_T$ is faithfully flat, preservation of $I$ descends to $T_D$: after an fppf cover any $T_D$-point lifts to $T_A$, and the equality defining preservation is an equality of closed-subscheme ideals. Thus $\operatorname{Lie}(I)$ is a $T_D$-stable line in $\operatorname{Lie}(D)$. Its character $\beta$ pulls back to $n\alpha$. This is nonzero because $X_A$ is torsion-free and $n>0$, so $\beta$ is a root of $D$. The uniqueness assertion of the root-subgroup node identifies $I=U_\beta$.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, image of a root subgroup and formula (146), p.485; 14.58, p.298.

proof.text:
Write $P(Z)=\sum_i b_iZ^i$, with $b_n=1$. The polynomial-quotient equivariance in step 2 gives $P(\alpha(t)Z)=\alpha(t)^nP(Z)$. Comparing coefficients over the universal torus gives $b_i
e0\Rightarrow i\alpha=n\alpha$. Since $\alpha
e0$ in the torsion-free lattice $X_A$, this forces $i=n$. Hence $P(Z)=Z^n$. Choose any prescribed parametrization $u_ eta$. The isomorphism from the quotient coordinate $\mathbf G_a$ to $U_ eta$ differs from $u_ eta$ by $Z\mapsto c_\alpha Z$, with $c_\alpha
e0$: a polynomial automorphism of the affine line over a field has degree one, since its degree times the degree of its inverse is one, and a group automorphism fixes zero. Consequently $f(u_\alpha(a))=u_ eta(c_\alpha a^n)$ over every commutative $F$-algebra, and $h( eta)=n\alpha$. These are identities of morphisms obtained from polynomial identities, so require no reducedness of the test algebra.

Additivity of $P(Z)=Z^n$ says $(X+Y)^n=X^n+Y^n$ in $F[X,Y]$. In characteristic zero, if $n>1$, the coefficient of $X^{n-1}Y$ would be the nonzero integer $n$, a contradiction; hence $n=1$. In characteristic $p>0$, write $n=p^r m$ with $p\nmid m$. The binomial identity $(X+Y)^{p^r}=X^{p^r}+Y^{p^r}$, iterated from the binomial coefficients for the prime $p$, reduces additivity to $(U+V)^m=U^m+V^m$: substitution $U=X^{p^r},V=Y^{p^r}$ is injective on polynomial rings, as distinct monomials remain distinct. If $m>1$, comparison of $U^{m-1}V$ gives $m=0$ in $F$, contrary to $p\nmid m$. Thus $m=1$. Set $e_\alpha=n$; it is a power of the characteristic exponent, including $1$ in characteristic zero.

source.place: Example 14.40, pp.292--293, specialized to a monomial; Proposition 23.5, p.485.

proof.text: The assignment $\alpha\mapsto\beta$ is injective. Indeed, if $\alpha,\gamma$ have the same image root, then $e_\alpha\alpha=e_\gamma\gamma$; reducedness in [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] makes positive rationally proportional roots equal. To see surjectivity without assuming separability of $f$, apply [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry] to the action of $A$ on $D$ by $a\cdot d=f(a)d$. Faithful flatness makes the orbit of $1$ all of $D$, and its stabilizer is the finite kernel, so $\dim A=\dim D$. For either group $G$, the charts in [lem-sfb-bruhat-longest-cell-charts], the product coordinates in [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates], and $B=U\rtimes T$ in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] give a dense open subscheme isomorphic to $\mathbf A^{2N}\times\mathbf G_m^r$, where $2N=|\Phi_G|$ and $r=\operatorname{rank}X^*(T)$. This is also a dense open of $\mathbf A^{2N+r}$. By [lem-weil-pbc-dense-open-dimension-comparison] and [lem-sf-noetherian-polynomial-dimension], $\dim G=2N+r=r+|\Phi_G|$. The ranks agree by step 1, so the two finite root sets have equal cardinality and the injection is a bijection. Injectivity of $h$ also gives $(-\alpha)\leftrightarrow(-\beta)$ and $e_{-\alpha}=e_\alpha$.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, pp.485--486; Corollary 21.13, p.430; Theorems 21.68 and 21.73, pp.445--447.

proof.text: For corresponding $\alpha,\beta$, take the largest subtori $T_\alpha\subseteq\ker\alpha$ and $T_\beta\subseteq\ker\beta$ from [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections]. Since $h(\beta)=e_\alpha\alpha$, $f_T(T_\alpha)\subseteq T_\beta$. This image equals $T_\beta$: the restriction has finite kernel, and the two subtori have equal rank $r-1$. These assertions can be checked in the character lattices using [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality] and the torus matrices in step 1: taking the kernel of a nonzero character lowers the rational rank by one, and a finite-kernel map has image of the same rank. The image map is faithfully flat by [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization]. Therefore $f(C_A(T_\alpha))\subseteq C_D(T_\beta)$: commutation with $T_\alpha$ implies commutation with all of $T_\beta$ after faithfully flat local lifting. Choose a representative $n_\alpha$ of the nontrivial rank-one Weyl element. Its image lies in $N_{D_\beta}(T_D)(F)$. Conjugation by this image is nontrivial: otherwise $s_\alpha h=h$, and $h_{\mathbf Q}$ being onto would force $s_\alpha=1$. The rank-one-reflections node says that there is exactly one nontrivial such Weyl element. Thus $f(n_\alpha)$ represents $s_\beta$ and $h s_\beta=s_\alpha h$.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, rank-one normalizer paragraph, p.486; Theorem 21.11(a),(d),(e), pp.428--430.

proof.text: For every $\chi\in X_D$, expand $h s_\beta(\chi)=s_\alpha h(\chi)$ using the reflection formulas of [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections]. Cancellation gives $\langle\chi,\beta^\vee\rangle h(\beta)=\langle h(\chi),\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$. Substitute $h(\beta)=e_\alpha\alpha$ and cancel the nonzero vector $\alpha$ in the free lattice to get $\langle h(\chi),\alpha^\vee\rangle=e_\alpha\langle\chi,\beta^\vee\rangle$. Composition of characters and cocharacters gives $\langle h(\chi),\nu\rangle=\langle\chi,f_*(\nu)\rangle$ directly from their definitions. The perfect lattice pairing in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] now yields $f_*(\alpha^\vee)=e_\alpha\beta^\vee$.

Set $K=\ker f$. By [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization], it is normal. Every $x\in K(F)$ is central in $A$ as a scheme-valued constant point. Indeed, apply [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry] to conjugation by $A$ on the finite scheme $K$. Its orbit is smooth and connected, being the image of connected $A$, and has dimension zero because $K$ is finite. Over the algebraically closed field it is a single reduced point; the faithfully flat orbit map therefore is the constant map with value $x$. This states that $x$ commutes with $A$ after every scalar extension. By [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer], $x\in T_A(F)$. Every point of the finite $F$-scheme $K$ has residue field $F$: its residue field is a finite-dimensional field extension of the algebraically closed field. Thus the whole topological support of $K$ lies in $T_A$. This support assertion does not assert that $K$ is reduced or central.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, kernel argument after the pairing calculation, p.486; Theorem 21.84, p.451.

proof.text: Choose a Borel $B_A$ containing $T_A$ by [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], and set $B_D=f(B_A)$ using [lem-sfb-quotient-borel-torus-images]. It contains $T_D$. For $\alpha$ positive in $B_A$, the image root group $U_\beta$ lies in $B_D$, hence its tangent weight $\beta$ is positive there. The bijection and the correspondence of negatives in step 5 therefore identify the two positive systems. By [lem-sfb-bruhat-longest-cell-charts], opposite Borels are obtained by conjugating by a longest Weyl representative. Translating its longest open cell by the inverse representative yields an open immersion $U^-\times T\times U^+\to G$, where $U^\pm$ are the opposite Borel radicals; this follows by replacing $u n_0 b$ by $n_0^{-1}u n_0 b$ and using $B=U^+\rtimes T$. This open cell contains $T$. By [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates], both $U^+$ and $U^-$ have ordered root coordinates. If every $e_\alpha=1$, the map $f$ is an isomorphism on each of these radicals: order the corresponding roots identically and the coordinate map is $(a_\alpha)\mapsto(c_\alpha a_\alpha)$. All constants are invertible. Consequently on these open cells $f$ is the product of those two isomorphisms and $f_T$.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, final kernel argument, p.486; Theorem 21.84 and Summary 21.86, pp.451--452.

proof.text: Assume every $e_\alpha=1$. Step 8 shows that $K$ factors through the open cell of step 9, since its entire support lies in $T_A$; a morphism whose inverse image of an open is its whole source factors through that open. In the product coordinates its equation $f(u^-tu^+)=1$ says $f(u^-)=1$, $f_T(t)=1$, $f(u^+)=1$ by uniqueness of the target open-cell coordinates. The radical maps are isomorphisms, so $u^-=u^+=1$. Thus $K=\ker f_T$ as subgroup schemes, including their nilpotents. For any test algebra and $t\in K$, step 3 gives $\alpha(t)=\beta(f_T(t))=1$ for every root, since $e_\alpha=1$. The scheme-theoretic centre description in [lem-sfb-reductive-centre-root-quotient] now implies $K\subseteq Z(A)$. This proves centrality.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, final centrality criterion, p.486; Theorem 21.84, p.451.

proof.text: Conversely assume $K$ central. It centralizes $T_A$, so [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer] gives $K\subseteq T_A$. For every root, $T_A\cap U_\alpha=1$ scheme-theoretically: for positive roots this follows from $B=U\rtimes T_A$ in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] and the inclusions in [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates]; for a negative root, conjugate this equality by a longest Weyl representative, which exchanges the two systems by [lem-sfb-bruhat-longest-cell-charts]. Thus $N_\alpha=K\cap U_\alpha$ is trivial. In the polynomial coordinates of steps 2--4, its coordinate ring is $F[Z]/(Z^{e_\alpha})$, of dimension $e_\alpha$, with basis $1,Z,\ldots,Z^{e_\alpha-1}$. The trivial group has coordinate ring $F$, so $e_\alpha=1$. This uses the full scheme kernel: in characteristic $p$, $Z^p$ has a nontrivial kernel even though its kernel has only one $F$-point. All clauses of the statement now follow; $f(U_\alpha)=U_\beta$ was a scheme-theoretic image equality already in step 2.

Shape: one commit, the item plus its report, no new nodes. This is the first delivery and there is no re-split note. The live node is still unsplit with the same statement and stmt_deps, so the statement is unchanged and no other group has superseded it. Step uses equal proof_deps exactly, there is no cycle, and the item has no SGA citation. Steps: (1) the image of T_A is T_D by the torus clause; h=f^* is injective because the coordinate map is injective; the kernel ring is F[coker h], so coker h is finite. (2) N_alpha is finite and proper; I=G_a/N_alpha comes from the factorization and polynomial-quotient nodes; the equivariance clause applies with eta=alpha; T_D normalizes I by fppf lifting; the weight beta satisfies beta∘f_T=n alpha≠0, and uniqueness in the root-subgroup node gives I=U_beta, without using a differential of f. (3)-(4) Coefficient comparison gives P=Z^n with n=p^r, and automorphisms of G_a are scalars; I checked both. (5) Injectivity uses reducedness of the root system. Surjectivity comes from a dimension count: dim A=dim D by the orbit lemma, and dim G=r+|Phi| from the big cell A^N x A^N x G_m^r. Milne omits this surjectivity; the delivery supplies it. (6)-(7) f(n_alpha) represents s_beta, because h_Q onto rules out a trivial action and the rank-one node gives uniqueness; the integral pairing then gives f_* alpha^vee=e beta^vee, which I verified, including in characteristic 2. (8) Points of K are central (orbit lemma) and lie in T_A (self-centralizer node). (9)-(10) The positive systems correspond; the open cell U^- x T x U^+ comes from opposite-Borel product coordinates; if every e=1 then K=ker f_T as schemes and lies in the intersection of the ker alpha, which is Z(A). (11) If K is central then K⊆T_A, T∩U_alpha=1, and F[Z]/(Z^e) has dimension e, so e=1. Edge cases checked: pure torus, Frobenius, SL_p→PGL_p, characteristic 0. Accepted tool uses: lem-weil-pbc-dense-open-dimension-comparison and the Mathlib leaf lem-sf-noetherian-polynomial-dimension.
